# ws (WebSocket Server)

The Node WebSocket implementation, `^8.21.1`. In [[stickfps]] it is the entire transport, serving
`/ws` on the same `express ^5.2.1` server that answers `/healthz`. It replaced geckos.io
(UDP-over-WebRTC) in the final build round — [[websocket-tcp-over-geckos-udp]].

## The wire format

Compact JSON frames shaped `{ e: event, d: data }` — event name plus payload, nothing else. Frames
are small by construction because the client only ever sends intent under
[[server-authoritative-netcode]], and the server's per-tick broadcast is a batched position snapshot
rather than one message per entity.

## Connection handling worth copying

- **Origin check in `verifyClient`**, against `CORS_ORIGIN`, before the upgrade completes. Cheaper
  than authenticating after the socket is open, and it is the reason [[stickfps]] keeps `express` and
  `cors` for a service with one HTTP route.
- **64 KB maximum payload.** A hard ceiling on any single frame limits the cheapest denial-of-service
  shape without any rate-limiting logic. (Per-connection *rate* limiting is still absent and is
  listed as a known gap.)
- **The server issues the identity.** Each connection gets a fresh `crypto.randomUUID()` delivered in
  a `connection-ready` frame, and the client's `connectToServer` promise resolves only once that id
  arrives. Anything the client believed about who it was before connecting is irrelevant — which is
  why {{supabase}}'s anonymous id is not the player id.
- **Reconnect with capped jittered exponential backoff**, 500 ms → 8 s. Jitter matters: without it
  every client dropped by one server restart returns in the same instant.

## The abstraction that made the swap cheap

Rather than rewrite gameplay code against `ws`, the build introduced `NetChannel` / `NetServer` —
an interface shaped to mirror **only the slice of the geckos.io API the code actually used**. No
gameplay code changed when the transport was replaced.

The transferable point is the sizing rule: the wrapper was written to the *observed usage*, not to
the vendor's full surface, and not speculatively in advance. A transport interface designed up front
to cover everything either transport might do would have been larger and would still have leaked.

## TCP, knowingly

WebSocket is TCP, so a lost packet blocks everything behind it — head-of-line blocking that UDP would
not have. Accepted explicitly and called "unnoticeable at hobby scale". Under this transport,
[[entity-interpolation]]'s 100 ms buffer is doing more work than it would over UDP.
